assumptions: The first target OEM is non-exempt, already retrieves the relevant telemetry, and controls or can authorize the cloud and identity stack needed for deployment.
The OEM and integrator will retain legal, disclosure, firmware, and product-security decisions while accepting a bounded customer-cloud module from an external specialist.
The proposed pricing, implementation margin, recurring margin, sales cycle, and renewal behavior are planning hypotheses rather than demonstrated economics.
No customer traction, partner commitment, or reusable second-product-line delivery evidence exists beyond the immutable packet.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A signed integrator resale or referral commitment and prepaid OEM statement of work, followed by measured delivery cost and time versus an internal-build quote, a paid second release or product line demonstrating asset reuse and renewal, and a qualified pipeline count of non-exempt OEMs with the specified access-surface gap.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: A near access-by-design deadline creates a credible release trigger, and focusing on vertical mappings, entitlement tests, logs, and accepted evidence is more substantive than selling commodity transport. The insight is weakened because the legal scope is narrower than a generic compliance thesis and much of the base stack already exists.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Missing a dated release or mishandling access rights can be consequential, giving the offer a plausible budget owner and paid event. However, there is no evidence that target OEMs have the stated gap, prefer outsourcing it, or will pay the proposed fees instead of extending their platform or incumbent-integrator work.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Prepayment, customer-hosted infrastructure, annual assurance, and separately scoped revalidation are sensible cash and scope controls. First implementations are explicitly labor-heavy, recurring gross margin and retention are hypotheses, CAC and payback are unknown, and reaching meaningful recurring scale requires many product-line subscriptions without an evidenced acquisition engine.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: The heat-pump and building-control product-line beachhead is precise enough to test and benefits from founder adjacency. Its economically reachable size is unknown and is narrowed by small-company exemptions, existing-stack requirements, OEM control requirements, and the need for an incumbent integrator willing to participate.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Accepted release packets and a vertical mapping library could earn a specialist position within a narrow equipment segment. Yet platform vendors and embedded integrators already control customer relationships and much of the technical stack, can bundle the missing layer, and may appropriate the specialist workflow.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful product line could lead to further releases, additional lines within an OEM, adjacent building-control categories, and eventually other connected-product verticals. Expansion is limited by vendor-specific semantics, security review, and legal classification work that may not transfer cleanly across products or sectors.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Versioned mappings, regression tests, operational logs, and embedded release acceptance could accumulate switching costs and delivery know-how. None of that compounding asset is established, while the generic interface is standardized and reproducible and better-positioned platforms or integrators can build comparable capabilities.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A bounded customer-cloud package may reduce release time and produce better evidence than an ad hoc internal implementation. No measured speed, cost, risk-transfer, or quality advantage is shown against an OEM's incumbent integrator, and the vendor does not own the legal judgments or core infrastructure.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The September 2026 access-by-design date provides a concrete and near-term catalyst, while unfinished standardization leaves room for implementation specialists. The same window also brings cybersecurity obligations and may favor established vendors already embedded in OEM release programs.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Integrator-led co-selling is more credible and founder-compatible than direct cold enterprise sales, and the family energy-business adjacency may open initial interviews. No integrator commitment, incentive proof, repeatable customer funnel, CAC, or route beyond the first partner is established, making the proposed gate a dependency rather than a channel asset today.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder can plausibly build and test one scoped data and identity implementation with AI leverage, 100000 PLN, and specialist support. Production access control, product-specific semantics, legal and security review, liability, OEM procurement, and support can exceed a part-time solo boundary, and the necessary integrator must accept a carefully bounded responsibility split.

highest_value_structural_change: Make the embedded integrator the contracted reseller and economic buyer through a white-label portfolio agreement with minimum annual product-line volume, standardized platform boundaries, and explicit liability ownership; this would align the current gatekeeper, reduce bespoke acquisition, and turn the partner from a potential substitute into a committed distribution asset.
main_structural_strength: The offer avoids competing on cheap transport and instead attaches payment and potential reuse to a concrete OEM release control point: vertical mappings, entitlement regression tests, request logs, and accepted evidence maintained in the customer cloud.
primary_score_limiter: The concept has not established that a sufficiently large set of non-exempt OEMs both has this gap and will outsource it at attractive recurring economics, while its sole proposed distribution partner is also capable of bundling the solution.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Major IoT platforms already provide secure identity, APIs, data, and fleet functions, and open Thing Description standards make the generic layer reproducible, so the incumbent platform or integrator can plausibly bundle the missing access and logging surface before a vertical release library compounds.
